sentences.text: Fossils of Qiaowanlong were discovered in the Yujinzi Basin of modern-day Gansu Province, China. The only known specimen consists of eight neck vertebrae, the right half of a pelvis, and unidentified bone fragments.

The genus name Qiaowanlong refers to the nearby cultural site of Qiaowan, derived from the Chinese words for 'bridge' and 'bend in a stream'. The species name kangxii honors the Kangxi Emperor, who reportedly dreamed of the Qiaowan area.
The longest known vertebra of Qiaowanlong, the seventh cervical vertebra, measures 45 cm in length.

Gregory S. Paul estimated Qiaowanlong to be about 12 meters long and weigh 6 tons, while Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi estimated it to be 20.7 meters long, 4.3 meters tall at the shoulder, and 13 tons in weight.
Qiaowanlong was formally described and named by Hai-Lu You and Da-Qing Li in 2009.

During the Early Cretaceous, the habitat of Qiaowanlong was likely a less arid environment near the coast of the Tethys Sea. The environment likely consisted of lowlands surrounded by narrow hills that allowed for easy movement of dinosaur populations.
Animals that may have coexisted with Qiaowanlong include the ornithopods Xuwulong and Jintasaurus, the tyrannosauroid Xiongguanlong, and the therizinosaur Suzhousaurus.
Qiaowanlong is classified within the unranked group Titanosauriformes. Later analyses placed Qiaowanlong within Euhelopodidae, suggesting a closer relationship to titanosaurs than to brachiosaurids.
Qiaowanlong was initially reported as the first brachiosaurid found in China, but later analysis showed it is more closely related to titanosauriforms like Euhelopus and Erketu.

Qiaowanlong lived during the late Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous period. Qiaowanlong lived approximately 100 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
The time range for Qiaowanlong is estimated between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
